description: Suffrage won but limited — what the 19th Amendment changed and what it left untouched.
content_html:
Women and the Vote

In August 1920, the 19th Amendment was ratified, completing a campaign for women’s suffrage that had been active since the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848. The amendment stated that the right to vote could not be denied on account of sex. It was a landmark achievement, but its practical impact was more limited than its supporters had hoped — and for Black women in the South, it changed almost nothing.

Key Fact

The 19th Amendment gave women the legal right to vote in federal and state elections from 1920. However, in the southern states, Jim Crow voter suppression tactics — literacy tests, poll taxes, and outright intimidation — that were used to prevent African American men from voting applied equally to African American women. White women in the South voted in significant numbers; Black women largely could not.

The Sheppard-Towner Act

The most significant piece of federal legislation directly connected to women’s political power in this period was the Sheppard-Towner Maternity Act, signed into law in November 1921. The act provided federal grants to states to establish prenatal and child welfare clinics. Women’s organisations, particularly the newly formed League of Women Voters, had lobbied hard for it, and many congressmen feared the consequences of opposing women’s welfare issues so soon after the 19th Amendment.

The Sheppard-Towner Act was genuinely significant: it created over 3,000 child health centres across the country, and infant mortality rates fell in states that participated. However, it was strongly opposed by the American Medical Association, which saw it as government interference in medicine, and by conservatives who feared it as a step towards socialism. Funding was repeatedly contested, and the act was allowed to expire in 1929 without renewal.

After the 19th Amendment, the suffrage movement split over strategy. The League of Women Voters, led by Carrie Chapman Catt, focused on educating women voters and working within the existing party system. Alice Paul’s National Woman’s Party took a more radical approach, introducing the Equal Rights Amendment in 1923 — a proposed constitutional amendment that would prohibit all sex-based discrimination. The ERA was repeatedly blocked in Congress through the 1920s; it was not passed until 1972, and even then it failed ratification.

Florence Kelley of the National Consumers League argued that the ERA would actually harm women workers by removing the protective labour legislation (such as limits on night shifts and maximum hours) that reformers had fought for. This tension between formal legal equality and protective special legislation divided women’s organisations throughout the 1920s and beyond.

Flappers and Changing Social Norms

The 1920s saw visible changes in women’s public behaviour, associated most strongly with the figure of the flapper. Young, urban, middle-class women cut their hair short, wore shorter skirts, danced at jazz clubs, and smoked in public. These visible changes shocked conservative opinion and suggested a broader loosening of Victorian social norms.

However, historians caution against overstating the significance of flapper culture. It was largely confined to urban, white, middle-class women. Most women — rural, working-class, or African American — saw little change in their economic position or their domestic expectations. Women workers remained concentrated in low-paid sectors: domestic service, garment manufacture, and clerical work. Married women faced widespread social pressure and often legal barriers to remaining in paid employment.

Key Fact

The Sheppard-Towner Maternity Act of 1921 was the first federal welfare law specifically aimed at women and children. It funded state child health clinics and reduced infant mortality where it operated. Opposition from the American Medical Association and conservative politicians, who saw it as “socialist,” led to its expiry in 1929 when Congress refused to renew funding.

Despite the vote and the Sheppard-Towner Act, much remained unchanged. Women were still largely excluded from professional careers in law and medicine by informal discrimination. The Equal Rights Amendment failed to pass, so legal inequalities in employment and property rights remained. African American women in the South were effectively denied the vote by Jim Crow measures. And the cultural freedoms of flapper culture were always limited to a minority — most American women in the 1920s were wives and mothers in rural or small-town environments where expectations had changed little.
exam_tip_html: Questions on women in the 1920s often require you to assess change and continuity. Avoid treating the 19th Amendment as a straightforward success story. The strongest answers will acknowledge the genuine significance of the vote and the Sheppard-Towner Act, while also explaining the limits of change — Jim Crow denial of the vote to Black women, the ERA’s failure, and the persistence of employment discrimination. When describing flappers, make sure you contextualise them as a minority experience rather than a universal change.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 19th Amendment (1920) gave women the legal right to vote, but Jim Crow voter suppression in the South meant that African American women were effectively denied this right in practice.
  • The Sheppard-Towner Act (1921) was a significant welfare achievement lobbied for by women’s organisations, but it expired in 1929 due to opposition from the medical establishment and conservatives.
  • The ERA, first introduced in 1923 by Alice Paul, and the social changes associated with flappers showed the aspirations of the era, but most American women — especially rural, working-class, and Black women — experienced limited practical change during the 1920s.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which women's lives changed after the ratification of the 19th Amendment in 1920.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each change scores 1 mark for identification and 1 additional mark for specific supporting detail. Example changes: women gained the legal right to vote in federal and state elections (1), enabling women’s organisations such as the League of Women Voters to lobby Congress directly for welfare legislation like the Sheppard-Towner Act (1); some urban middle-class women adopted flapper culture (1), with shorter skirts, bobbed hair, and greater social freedom in public spaces such as jazz clubs (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the 19th Amendment did not achieve full equality for women in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully explained with specific evidence — e.g. Jim Crow measures (literacy tests, poll taxes, intimidation) prevented African American women in the South from exercising their new vote; and women remained in low-paid employment sectors, with the ERA defeated in Congress, meaning legal employment discrimination persisted. Secure: Both reasons explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both reasons identified but not explained with causal link.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Sheppard-Towner Act was significant for women in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the act’s significance in multiple dimensions — as the first federal welfare law specifically addressing women and children; as evidence of women’s organisations’ political influence post-19th Amendment; as a practical health benefit (over 3,000 clinics, reduced infant mortality). Also acknowledges its limits (opposed by AMA and conservatives, expired 1929). Secure: Two or more dimensions explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One dimension explained, others named. Emerging: General statement without specific evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Equal Rights Amendment first proposed in 1923.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: The ERA was introduced by Alice Paul of the National Woman’s Party (1); it proposed a constitutional ban on all sex-based discrimination in law (1). Feature 2: The ERA was opposed by some women’s organisations as well as conservatives (1); Florence Kelley argued it would remove protective labour legislation that benefited women workers (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the 1920s was a decade of genuine progress for women in the United States? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that acknowledges real gains (19th Amendment, Sheppard-Towner Act, changing social norms) while explaining significant limits (Jim Crow denial of vote to Black women, ERA failure, persistent employment discrimination, domestic expectations largely unchanged for most women); uses specific evidence throughout and engages with at least one interpretation. Secure: Clear argument addressing both progress and its limits with relevant evidence. Developing: Some awareness of both sides with basic evidence; may be one-sided. Emerging: Descriptive account without structured argument. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of women's progress in the 1920s. Interpretation A argues the decade marked a revolution in women's status. Interpretation B argues that visible cultural changes disguised the persistence of inequality. How far do the interpretations differ, and what might explain their differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies key points of difference (scope of change, which women benefited, legal vs. social change); uses own knowledge to evaluate both (e.g. the 19th Amendment and flapper culture support A; denial of vote to Black women, ERA failure, and workplace discrimination support B); explains why interpretations differ (different evidence focus, urban vs. rural experience). Secure: Explains differences with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Identifies some differences and supports one. Emerging: Summarises both without explaining differences.

glossary_terms.definition: The constitutional amendment ratified in August 1920 that granted women the right to vote in all US elections.
A 1921 federal law funding state maternal and child health programmes — the first US welfare legislation aimed specifically at women and children.
A non-partisan organisation founded in 1920 by Carrie Chapman Catt to encourage women to exercise their new voting rights and engage in civic life.
A term for young women of the 1920s who challenged traditional expectations through shorter skirts, bobbed hair, dancing, and greater social independence.
